title: ActionOPD: Distilling Decisions, Not Tokens

paper.title: ActionOPD: Distilling Decisions, Not Tokens
paper.abstract: Abstract Distilling capable language-model agents into smaller models requires aligning the student’s behavior with the teacher’s. This raises a fundamental question: at which states and at what granularity should this alignment be performed? Offline imitation provides dense but token-specific supervision and can suffer from state-distribution mismatch. Token-level on-policy distillation (OPD) addresses this mismatch but typically requires teacher token probabilities and compatible tokenization. We argue that semantic actions provide a natural unit of supervision for agent distillation. We introduce ActionOPD, an action-level on-policy distillation method motivated by maximizing expected teacher-action likelihood at student-encountered states. At each such state, ActionOPD samples actions from both the student and a black-box teacher, rewarding student actions according to their semantic agreement with the sampled teacher actions. Through policy optimization, ActionOPD aligns the student’s action-level behavior with the teacher’s decisions without requiring reproduction of teacher-written reasoning or access to teacher token probabilities. Training Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B with two teachers on diverse, curated tool-use tasks yields average gains of 3.3–6.9 percentage points across four out-of-distribution benchmarks. ActionOPD scales favorably with student size and teacher capability, without requiring the teacher and student to share a model family or tokenizer. On τ 2 \tau^{2} -bench, ActionOPD achieves competitive performance against offline distillation and token-level OPD. We further explore Self-ActionOPD with a same-model teacher and privileged context. These results establish ActionOPD as a promising approach to agent distillation.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Figure 1: Student–teacher scaling of ActionOPD. Larger students attain higher final averages. DeepSeek-V4-Flash yields higher student averages than Qwen3.7-Flash. Language models are increasingly deployed as agents that communicate with users, maintain state, and act through external tools ( Yao et al., 2023 ; Yao et al., 2025 ) . In these interactions, an agent’s decisions shape subsequent observations and the states it encounters. Distilling capable but expensive frontier agents into smaller models therefore raises two questions: at which states should the teacher supervise the student, and at what granularity should their behavior be aligned? Distillation methods address these questions differently. Offline distillation provides dense supervision by fitting teacher-generated sequences ( Kim and Rush, 2016 ) , but can face teacher–student state-distribution mismatch ( Ross et al., 2011 ) . Token-level on-policy distillation (OPD) supervises student-generated sequences using teacher token probabilities, reducing mismatch while typically requiring compatible tokenization ( Agarwal et al., 2024 ; Gu et al., 2024 ) . Both supervise tokens without explicitly matching action semantics (Figure 2 ). Figure 2: Supervision for agent learning. Offline distillation (KD) imitates teacher tokens at teacher-induced states. Token-level OPD compares token distributions along student-generated interactions. Outcome-based RL uses terminal feedback. ActionOPD instead rewards semantic agreement with teacher actions at student-encountered states. Here, we sample only one response per state for demonstration. For implementation, we expand the sampled teacher multiset and student state group. Our key observation is that semantic actions provide a natural unit of supervision for agent distillation. A tool call expresses a decision through its tool name and arguments; a natural-language response conveys communicative intent and information. The same decision can be realized through different wording and reasoning. This shifts the objective from reproducing a particular teacher sequence to increasing the likelihood of its underlying action. We introduce ActionOPD , an action-level on-policy distillation method motivated by maximizing expected teacher-action likelihood at student-encountered states. Here, likelihood is the total probability mass of student outputs that semantically match a teacher action, not the probability of reproducing one teacher-written sequence. This objective yields a REINFORCE-form policy gradient with action-level semantic agreement as reward ( Williams, 1992 ) . In practice, ActionOPD samples actions from the teacher and responses from the current student policy, rewarding student responses according to their semantic agreement with teacher actions. It requires only generation access to a black-box teacher, not teacher token probabilities or tokenizer alignment. The resulting action-level rewards train the student’s own reasoning and action tokens without imposing teacher-written reasoning as a token-level imitation target. We train Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B students using teachers from two model families on curated tool-use tasks from Agent World Model (AWM) and EnvScaler ( Wang et al., 2026b ; Song et al., 2026 ) . All four configurations improve average performance across four out-of-distribution agent benchmarks. ActionOPD scales favorably with student size and teacher capability: larger students achieve higher final averages, and DeepSeek-V4-Flash yields higher student averages than Qwen3.7-Flash at both sizes (Figure 1 ). Comparisons on τ 2 \tau^{2} -bench ( Barres et al., 2025 ) show competitive performance against offline distillation and token-level OPD. Ablation studies support the effectiveness of semantic action supervision. We further explore Self-ActionOPD, in which a same-model teacher receives privileged task information. This extension suggests a path toward agent self-improvement through action-level self-distillation.

sections.heading: Contributions.
sections.text: Our contributions are threefold: • We introduce ActionOPD, an action-level on-policy distillation method that decouples teacher decision supervision from student token realization, enabling distillation from black-box teachers without teacher token probabilities or tokenizer alignment. • We demonstrate ActionOPD’s applicability across teacher families and empirical scaling with student size and teacher capability. All tested configurations improve the four-benchmark average over their corresponding base models by 3.3–6.9 percentage points. • We show that ActionOPD achieves competitive performance against offline distillation and token-level OPD while requiring only generation access to the teacher.

sections.heading: 3 Experiments
sections.text: We evaluate ActionOPD’s cross-benchmark generalization, student–teacher scaling, and performance relative to other distillation methods. We then use ablations and case studies to examine its components and decision-making behavior, and explore Self-ActionOPD with privileged teacher context.

sections.heading: Training data.
sections.text: We trained on Agent World Model (AWM; Wang et al., 2026b ) and EnvScaler ( Song et al., 2026 ) . AWM provides executable tools and persistent backend state; EnvScaler adds a simulated user to the interaction loop. The curated pool comprised 5,942 AWM tasks from 794 environments and 755 EnvScaler tasks from 49 environments : 6,697 tasks in total. Screening assessed environment integrity and static task feasibility, without requiring successful expert rollouts (Appendix B.1 ).

sections.heading: Models and training.
sections.text: We paired Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B students ( Yang et al., 2025 ) with Qwen3.7-Flash ( Alibaba Cloud, 2026 ) and DeepSeek-V4-Flash ( DeepSeek-AI, 2026 ) action teachers in a 2 × 2 2\times 2 design. Each configuration used 100 training steps and 64 task starts per step (59 AWM, 5 EnvScaler), with N = 4 N=4 student candidates, K = 3 K=3 teacher samples per state, and frequency bonus scale λ = 0.5 \lambda=0.5 . Task starts could revisit tasks in the curated pool. We report the final checkpoints, with Base denoting the corresponding student before ActionOPD training. Appendix B.2 details settings and auxiliary models.

sections.heading: Evaluation.
sections.text: We evaluated transfer on BFCL Multi-turn ( Patil et al., 2025 ) , ToolSandbox ’s verified-local-only subset ( Lu et al., 2025 ) , AppWorld Normal and Challenge ( Trivedi et al., 2024 ) , and τ 2 \tau^{2} -bench Airline, Retail, and Telecom ( Barres et al., 2025 ) . These tasks were excluded from AWM/EnvScaler training. Students used greedy decoding without teacher-guided action selection. Appendix B.3 details coverage, trials, and interaction protocols.

sections.heading: 3.2 Main results
sections.text: Table 1 compares distilled students with base models and directly evaluated teachers.

sections.heading: Cross-benchmark generalization.
sections.text: After training on AWM and EnvScaler, all four configurations improved the four-benchmark average over their base models by 3.3–6.9 percentage points. Gains extended across BFCL accuracy, ToolSandbox similarity, and AppWorld task completion. These gains on benchmarks excluded from training demonstrate that action-level distillation transfers beyond the training environments, improving average performance across diverse agent tasks.

sections.heading: Scaling with student size.
sections.text: With either teacher, Qwen3-8B achieved a higher final average than Qwen3-4B under the same task-start and training-step budgets. We used the same candidate count, teacher sample count, and reward formulation for both students. This pattern supports empirical scaling across the two tested sizes, with larger students yielding stronger distilled agents.

sections.heading: Scaling with teacher capability.
sections.text: DeepSeek-V4-Flash achieved a higher direct-evaluation average than Qwen3.7-Flash and yielded higher student averages at both sizes (Figure 1 ), supporting empirical scaling with teacher capability. The DeepSeek-to-Qwen results also demonstrate effective cross-family distillation through an action-level interface that requires neither a shared model family nor tokenizer alignment. This allows teacher selection to prioritize decision quality rather than compatibility with the student’s token space.

sections.heading: 3.4 Ablation studies
sections.text: Ablations shared the settings in Section 3.3 , with N = 4 N=4 and K = 3 K=3 . Validity Reward replaced the semantic training reward with action validity, while retaining semantic scores for action selection. Binary Reward removed the frequency bonus from Equation 6 , using binary agreement for both training and action selection. Random Commit retained ActionOPD’s reward but selected uniformly from all candidates, including invalid or zero-reward actions. Appendix B.4 details the variants and their effects on trainable state groups. Table 3 reports results on the training set and 100 held-out tasks. ActionOPD outperforms all three variants in average single-trial success on both splits, supporting the combined design. The largest drop occurs with Validity Reward, which assigns identical rewards to all valid candidates and thus provides no learning signal in all-valid groups. Semantic rewards can instead distinguish these candidates by their agreement with teacher actions, highlighting the value of supervising action meaning beyond protocol compliance. sections.heading: 3.5 Pattern analysis
sections.text: We compared Qwen3-4B Base with the same student after 100 ActionOPD steps using DeepSeek-V4-Flash as teacher. Each selected case has at least two additional successes after training over the first four trials. Table 4 summarizes one Base-failure/ActionOPD-success pair matched by task and trial index in each Tau domain, using replies, tool calls, and environment results. In these cases, the student respected policy constraints, distinguished information sources from operation targets, and followed through on promised actions. These changes highlight the value of ActionOPD’s semantic action supervision for task-appropriate behavior.

sections.heading: 3.6 Self-ActionOPD
sections.text: We further examine whether a model can provide useful action-level supervision for itself when given privileged task information. Self-ActionOPD shared current Qwen3-4B weights between teacher and student, as in OPSD ( Zhao et al., 2026 ) , but independently sampled their responses. Teacher responses were refreshed from the updated shared model at each collection step and held fixed during subsequent policy optimization. The student received only public interaction context, whereas the teacher additionally received action guidance, summaries of private user goals and constraints, and reference actions and target outcomes. Training used action-agreement rewards on student-generated candidates only. Appendix B.5 provides implementation details. After 50 steps, Self-ActionOPD improved test average pass 1 / pass 4 \mathrm{pass}^{1}/\mathrm{pass}^{4} over Base by 4.8/2.5 percentage points (Table 5 ). Single-trial success also improved across all three domains. Unlike the privileged-teacher reference, the trained student was evaluated using only public context, showing that the student retained benefits from the privileged guidance after training. Together, these results support the feasibility of using a same-model teacher given privileged context for action-level distillation.

sections.heading: Distillation and self-distillation.
sections.text: Classical distillation transfers predictive distributions ( Hinton et al., 2015 ) , while sequence distillation imitates generated outputs ( Kim and Rush, 2016 ) . Offline imitation uses token-level losses on fixed demonstrations that may not cover student-induced prefixes. GKD and MiniLLM instead supervise student-generated sequences through token-level divergences ( Agarwal et al., 2024 ; Gu et al., 2024 ) . These objectives require teacher distributions or sampled-token log-probabilities. Guidance can become unreliable under prefix drift or special-token mismatch ( Fu et al., 2026 ) . Cross-tokenizer OPD transfers probabilistic supervision through explicit alignment ( Niu et al., 2026 ; Wang et al., 2026a ) . Privileged self-distillation augments teacher context: On-Policy Self-Distillation (OPSD) minimizes token-level divergence on student rollouts using a shared-weight teacher conditioned on reference solutions ( Zhao et al., 2026 ) . SDPO distills feedback-conditioned predictions ( Hübotter et al., 2026 ) , while privileged-information distillation studies shared-parameter training, including on-policy reverse KL ( Penaloza et al., 2026 ) . Self-ActionOPD instead uses sampled-action agreement.

sections.heading: Black-box and semantic distillation.
sections.text: GAD jointly trains a discriminator to reward teacher-like responses ( Ye et al., 2025 ) , whereas ROPD evaluates responses against rubrics derived from teacher–student contrasts ( Fang et al., 2026 ) . On-policy Verbal Distillation (OVD) uses verbal teacher scores to evaluate reasoning quality at step and trajectory levels ( Xiong et al., 2026 ) . OmniOPD compares selected student reasoning chunks with teacher continuations sampled at student prefixes ( Zhou et al., 2026 ) . MENTOR rewards trajectory-wide tool-set agreement, final correctness, and execution validity ( Choi et al., 2025 ) . Action Semantics Learning (ASL) derives a semantic-agreement policy gradient and uses a world model to compare UI transitions induced by generated and reference actions. Its RL variant combines teacher-action agreement with environment rewards ( Tang et al., 2026 ) . ActionOPD instead matches immediate tool calls or communicative responses against teacher samples at the same state. Its matcher is instructed to assess agreement, not correctness. ActionOPD requires no reasoning-text matching, complete reference trajectories, or terminal rewards.

sections.heading: Interactive agent learning and process supervision.
sections.text: DAgger queries experts at learner-visited states ( Ross et al., 2011 ) . SCoRe provides local teacher corrections before supervised and short-horizon RL refinement ( Lyu et al., 2026 ) . Guided-OPD gradually withdraws teacher turns through a rollout curriculum; ATOD combines OPD and RL with annealed coefficients and turn-level weighting ( Li et al., 2026 ; Tan et al., 2026 ) . GiGPO retrospectively groups repeated states across trajectories and derives relative advantages from returns ( Feng et al., 2025 ) . ActionOPD scores directly sampled same-state candidates against a shared teacher multiset, without estimating returns.

sections.heading: 5 Conclusion and limitations
sections.text: ActionOPD decouples teacher decision supervision from student token realization through semantic agreement at student-encountered states, requiring only generation access to the teacher. Across tested configurations, it improves average performance on unseen benchmarks, with higher final averages from larger students and stronger teachers. ActionOPD also achieves competitive performance against offline distillation and token-level OPD. Ablations support semantic rewards over validity rewards. Self-ActionOPD improves held-out performance using a same-model teacher with privileged context, highlighting a potential path toward agent self-improvement. Together, these findings support semantic actions as a unit of supervision for agent distillation. Three limitations warrant attention. First, agreement does not guarantee correctness: teacher errors or suboptimal decisions can become learning targets. Second, LLM matching of communicative responses and tool-argument differences can produce false positives or negatives, misassigning rewards. Third, fixed-size teacher and student sample sets may contain few semantically matching actions when plausible decisions are dispersed, as may occur in long-horizon interactions. Increasing K K and N N could improve coverage at greater generation and matching cost, but the benefit in this regime remains untested.

The use of language models for task screening, teacher supervision, semantic matching, and user simulation is documented in the experimental protocol. sections.heading: Visible information and native tools.
sections.text: In standard ActionOPD, teacher and student receive the same retained public context and tool schemas through their native chat templates. Each teacher sample contains one immediate action. Hidden simulator state, verifier code, task solutions, and private user-simulator instructions are excluded. Self-ActionOPD adds the inputs in Appendix B.5 . Tools are exposed directly, without list_tools / call_tool wrappers. Multiple student tool calls violate the single-action protocol; only the teacher’s first call is retained when its output contains several.

sections.heading: Teacher sampling and validation.
sections.text: The teacher multiset is fixed before student generation. Each of three requested samples permits two retries for parser/schema-invalid output; valid samples are retained without regeneration. This filters protocol validity, not task success. A nonempty partial multiset can supervise a group, retaining nominal K = 3 K=3 in the bonus denominator. With two retained copies of A A , a matching student response receives 1.25 1.25 at λ = 0.5 \lambda=0.5 . With no valid samples, collection ends without a student group or policy-failure label. Retries and partial retention differ from independent sampling in Section 2.2 .

sections.heading: Caching.
sections.text: Teacher-cache keys include task/state context, tools, teacher/provider, prompt and protocol versions, decoding settings, and history-dependent state. Retained samples preserve multiplicity. Reuse does not provide fresh independent draws. Matcher-cache keys include the action pair, evidence, model, and prompt.

sections.heading: Context management.
sections.text: Native chat templates retain fixed task/system content and complete tool schemas, dropping the oldest removable exchanges until the prompt fits its token budget. The standard teacher uses the same retained public context; Self-ActionOPD has an additional teacher-only prompt allowance (Appendix B.5 ). If protected content cannot fit, the rollout terminates without truncating tool definitions or fabricating an action. Prompt construction leaves the environment’s full interaction history intact.

sections.text: All configurations use the same 178-task Tau training set and Qwen3-4B initialization. KD, OPD, and standard ActionOPD use Qwen3-32B as action teacher. Each step starts eight tasks per domain, and Tables 2 and 3 report step 50. Their ActionOPD rows reuse one run.

sections.heading: ActionOPD.
sections.text: The reference configuration uses Equation 6 with K = 3 K=3 , λ = 0.5 \lambda=0.5 , and uniform tie-breaking among maximum-reward candidates.

sections.heading: Validity Reward.
sections.text: Training assigns + 1 +1 to valid actions and − 1 -1 to invalid output or transfer-protocol violations. Teacher sampling and semantic matching remain active for ActionOPD’s commitment rule, not training rewards. All-valid groups are masked as equal-reward groups, so this variant changes the number and composition of trainable groups as well as removing semantic reward distinctions.

sections.heading: Binary Reward.
sections.text: With the same three teacher samples, λ = 0 \lambda=0 gives + 1 +1 for any match, zero for valid non-matches, and − 1 -1 for invalid actions. This reward also governs commitment, changing both learning signals and ties relative to ActionOPD.

sections.heading: Random Commit.
sections.text: Rewards follow ActionOPD, but commitment is uniform over all four candidates, including invalid and zero-reward actions. There is no success-based resampling. All candidates in retained groups contribute to training. A transfer notification without the preceding transfer call is treated as invalid output with reward − 1 -1 . Equal-reward groups produce no learning signal.

sections.heading: KD: successful teacher-trajectory imitation.
sections.text: For each task start, Qwen3-32B independently generated four complete trajectories; only successful ones entered SFT. Following output imitation ( Kim and Rush, 2016 ) , loss covers all teacher-generated reasoning and action/message tokens, while user turns and tool observations provide context only. Thus outcome labels filter demonstrations, but do not supply a policy-gradient reward.

sections.heading: OPD: sampled-token reverse-KL.
sections.text: OPD collected four student trajectories per task start. The teacher scored student-sampled tokens at their corresponding prefixes for sampled-token reverse-KL supervision ( Fu et al., 2026 ) . It requires teacher log-probabilities and a compatible token space, but not full-vocabulary distributions.

sections.heading: Collection budgets.
sections.text: KD and OPD collect four trajectories per task start; ActionOPD samples four candidates per state and executes one, while all candidates in retained groups contribute to training. Trajectory lengths, teacher generation/scoring, matching costs, and KD filtering differ. Equal task starts and collection steps therefore do not equalize retained examples, tokens, teacher queries, or compute.

sections.heading: Current-weight teacher, fixed update targets.
sections.text: Self-ActionOPD used Qwen3-4B in both roles, with eight task starts per Tau domain per step. We report results at step 50. Four student candidates and three teacher samples were independently generated from the same current parameters. Teacher samples and matching results remained fixed during optimization. Subsequent collection used updated shared parameters. Self-teacher caches were cleared at each collection step. Table 8 specifies generation settings. During Self-ActionOPD training, both roles used a 32,768-token context window and a 4,096-token response limit. Student and teacher prompts were capped at 24,576 and 28,672 tokens, respectively, providing an additional 4,096 tokens for teacher-only inputs. Teacher outputs and private prompt tokens were excluded from the student loss. Only student-generated candidate tokens received the action-level signal.

sections.heading: Teacher guidance and privileged information.
sections.text: The student received the domain policy, available tools, and observed interaction history. Additional teacher guidance covered immediate actions, preconditions, authorization, clarification, and avoiding repetition. Telecom device operations were rendered as user-facing instructions rather than user-tool syntax. This conversion added no private facts. Privileged task information comprised reviewed summaries of private goals, constraints, preferences, and known/unknown information, including facts not yet disclosed in dialogue. It also supplied reference tool names and arguments, customer-side operations, target states, and required messages from evaluation criteria. These inputs did not replace required public confirmation or execution evidence. They were withheld from the student and matcher, although they could affect which student actions were rewarded. The trained student was evaluated without privileged inputs.

Project Page Code Models Abstract Distilling capable language-model agents into smaller models requires aligning the student’s behavior with the teacher’s. This raises a fundamental question: at which states and at what granularity should this alignment be performed? Offline imitation provides dense but token-specific supervision and can suffer from state-distribution mismatch. Token-level on-policy distillation (OPD) addresses this mismatch but typically requires teacher token probabilities and compatible tokenization. We argue that semantic actions provide a natural unit of supervision for agent distillation. We introduce ActionOPD, an action-level on-policy distillation method motivated by maximizing expected teacher-action likelihood at student-encountered states. At each such state, ActionOPD samples actions from both the student and a black-box teacher, rewarding student actions according to their semantic agreement with the sampled teacher actions. Through policy optimization, ActionOPD aligns the student’s action-level behavior with the teacher’s decisions without requiring reproduction of teacher-written reasoning or access to teacher token probabilities. Training Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B with two teachers on diverse, curated tool-use tasks yields average gains of 3.3–6.9 percentage points across four out-of-distribution benchmarks. ActionOPD scales favorably with student size and teacher capability, without requiring the teacher and student to share a model family or tokenizer. On τ 2 \tau^{2} -bench, ActionOPD achieves competitive performance against offline distillation and token-level OPD. We further explore Self-ActionOPD with a same-model teacher and privileged context. These results establish ActionOPD as a promising approach to agent distillation. 1 Introduction Figure 1: Student–teacher scaling of ActionOPD. Larger students attain higher final averages. DeepSeek-V4-Flash yields higher student averages than Qwen3.7-Flash. Language models are increasingly deployed as agents that communicate with users, maintain state, and act through external tools ( Yao et al., 2023 ; Yao et al., 2025 ) . In these interactions, an agent’s decisions shape subsequent observations and the states it encounters. Distilling capable but expensive frontier agents into smaller models therefore raises two questions: at which states should the teacher supervise the student, and at what granularity should their behavior be aligned? Distillation methods address these questions differently. Offline distillation provides dense supervision by fitting teacher-generated sequences ( Kim and Rush, 2016 ) , but can face teacher–student state-distribution mismatch ( Ross et al., 2011 ) . Token-level on-policy distillation (OPD) supervises student-generated sequences using teacher token probabilities, reducing mismatch while typically requiring compatible tokenization ( Agarwal et al., 2024 ; Gu et al., 2024 ) . Both supervise tokens without explicitly matching action semantics (Figure 2 ). Figure 2: Supervision for agent learning. Offline distillation (KD) imitates teacher tokens at teacher-induced states. Token-level OPD compares token distributions along student-generated interactions. Outcome-based RL uses terminal feedback. ActionOPD instead rewards semantic agreement with teacher actions at student-encountered states. Here, we sample only one response per state for demonstration. For implementation, we expand the sampled teacher multiset and student state group. Our key observation is that semantic actions provide a natural unit of supervision for agent distillation. A tool call expresses a decision through its tool name and arguments; a natural-language response conveys communicative intent and information. The same decision can be realized through different wording and reasoning. This shifts the objective from reproducing a particular teacher sequence to increasing the likelihood of its underlying action. We introduce ActionOPD , an action-level on-policy distillation method motivated by maximizing expected teacher-action likelihood at student-encountered states. Here, likelihood is the total probability mass of student outputs that semantically match a teacher action, not the probability of reproducing one teacher-written sequence. This objective yields a REINFORCE-form policy gradient with action-level semantic agreement as reward ( Williams, 1992 ) . In practice, ActionOPD samples actions from the teacher and responses from the current student policy, rewarding student responses according to their semantic agreement with teacher actions. It requires only generation access to a black-box teacher, not teacher token probabilities or tokenizer alignment. The resulting action-level rewards train the student’s own reasoning and action tokens without imposing teacher-written reasoning as a token-level imitation target. We train Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B students using teachers from two model families on curated tool-use tasks from Agent World Model (AWM) and EnvScaler ( Wang et al., 2026b ; Song et al., 2026 ) . All four configurations improve average performance across four out-of-distribution agent benchmarks. ActionOPD scales favorably with student size and teacher capability: larger students achieve higher final averages, and DeepSeek-V4-Flash yields higher student averages than Qwen3.7-Flash at both sizes (Figure 1 ). Comparisons on τ 2 \tau^{2} -bench ( Barres et al., 2025 ) show competitive performance against offline distillation and token-level OPD. Ablation studies support the effectiveness of semantic action supervision. We further explore Self-ActionOPD, in which a same-model teacher receives privileged task information. This extension suggests a path toward agent self-improvement through action-level self-distillation. Contributions. Our contributions are threefold: • We introduce ActionOPD, an action-level on-policy distillation method that decouples teacher decision supervision from student token realization, enabling distillation from black-box teachers without teacher token probabilities or tokenizer alignment. • We demonstrate ActionOPD’s applicability across teacher families and empirical scaling with student size and teacher capability. All tested configurations improve the four-benchmark average over their corresponding base models by 3.3–6.9 percentage points. • We show that ActionOPD achieves competitive performance against offline distillation and token-level OPD while requiring only generation access to the teacher. 2 ActionOPD A language-model agent alternates between generating responses and receiving environment observations. At step t t , its visible state s t s_{t} contains the task, tools, and retained interaction history. Its response y t y_{t} realizes a semantic action a t = ϕ s t ​ ( y t ) a_{t}=\phi_{s_{t}}(y_{t}) . Classical distillation transfers predictive distributions ( Hinton et al., 2015 ) , while sequence distillation imitates generated outputs ( Kim and Rush, 2016 ) . Offline imitation uses token-level losses on fixed demonstrations that may not cover student-induced prefixes. GKD and MiniLLM instead supervise student-generated sequences through token-level divergences ( Agarwal et al., 2024 ; Gu et al., 2024 ) . These objectives require teacher distributions or sampled-token log-probabilities. Guidance can become unreliable under prefix drift or special-token mismatch ( Fu et al., 2026 ) . Cross-tokenizer OPD transfers probabilistic supervision through explicit alignment ( Niu et al., 2026 ; Wang et al., 2026a ) . Privileged self-distillation augments teacher context: On-Policy Self-Distillation (OPSD) minimizes token-level divergence on student rollouts using a shared-weight teacher conditioned on reference solutions ( Zhao et al., 2026 ) . SDPO distills feedback-conditioned predictions ( Hübotter et al., 2026 ) , while privileged-information distillation studies shared-parameter training, including on-policy reverse KL ( Penaloza et al., 2026 ) . Self-ActionOPD instead uses sampled-action agreement. Black-box and semantic distillation. GAD jointly trains a discriminator to reward teacher-like responses ( Ye et al., 2025 ) , whereas ROPD evaluates responses against rubrics derived from teacher–student contrasts ( Fang et al., 2026 ) . On-policy Verbal Distillation (OVD) uses verbal teacher scores to evaluate reasoning quality at step and trajectory levels ( Xiong et al., 2026 ) . OmniOPD compares selected student reasoning chunks with teacher continuations sampled at student prefixes ( Zhou et al., 2026 ) . MENTOR rewards trajectory-wide tool-set agreement, final correctness, and execution validity ( Choi et al., 2025 ) . Action Semantics Learning (ASL) derives a semantic-agreement policy gradient and uses a world model to compare UI transitions induced by generated and reference actions. Its RL variant combines teacher-action agreement with environment rewards ( Tang et al., 2026 ) . ActionOPD instead matches immediate tool calls or communicative responses against teacher samples at the same state. Its matcher is instructed to assess agreement, not correctness. ActionOPD requires no reasoning-text matching, complete reference trajectories, or terminal rewards. Interactive agent learning and process supervision. DAgger queries experts at learner-visited states ( Ross et al., 2011 ) . SCoRe provides local teacher corrections before supervised and short-horizon RL refinement ( Lyu et al., 2026 ) . Guided-OPD gradually withdraws teacher turns through a rollout curriculum; ATOD combines OPD and RL with annealed coefficients and turn-level weighting ( Li et al., 2026 ; Tan et al., 2026 ) . GiGPO retrospectively groups repeated states across trajectories and derives relative advantages from returns ( Feng et al., 2025 ) . ActionOPD scores directly sampled same-state candidates against a shared teacher multiset, without estimating returns. 5 Conclusion and limitations ActionOPD decouples teacher decision supervision from student token realization through semantic agreement at student-encountered states, requiring only generation access to the teacher. Across tested configurations, it improves average performance on unseen benchmarks, with higher final averages from larger students and stronger teachers. ActionOPD also achieves competitive performance against offline distillation and token-level OPD. Ablations support semantic rewards over validity rewards. Self-ActionOPD improves held-out performance using a same-model teacher with privileged context, highlighting a potential path toward agent self-improvement. Together, these findings support semantic actions as a unit of supervision for agent distillation. Three limitations warrant attention. First, agreement does not guarantee correctness: teacher errors or suboptimal decisions can become learning targets. Second, LLM matching of communicative responses and tool-argument differences can produce false positives or negatives, misassigning rewards. Third, fixed-size teacher and student sample sets may contain few semantically matching actions when plausible decisions are dispersed, as may occur in long-horizon interactions. Increasing K K and N N could improve coverage at greater generation and matching cost, but the benefit in this regime remains untested.
